Trust Trust

The long version.

Every claim on the Trust page, with the full reasoning behind it. If you are checking our work rather than skimming it, this is the page you want.

No Company Publishes This Section

Where we fall short.

Every privacy page tells you what a company is good at. Here is the other half. If any of this changes, we will change it here on the same day.

Your agent asks before it changes anything, and that only helps if you read before you approve.

When your agent wants to change a calendar you’ve connected (create, move, or delete an event) or send an email or a text, it doesn’t just do it. It proposes the exact action first, and the app itself enforces the shape rather than politely instructing the AI: an email or text goes out only when you press Send on the draft, and a calendar change can never apply on the turn that proposed it, can only apply exactly as proposed, and can never apply while you are away. One honest seam in that: on the calendar side, the AI is what reads your later message as a yes before it calls apply, so what the app guarantees is the structure, and what the AI supplies is the judgment. It proposes; you dispose.

Here is the honest limit that remains. The gate stops your agent from doing something you didn’t approve. It cannot stop it from proposing the wrong thing: if it misreads what you wanted and you approve without looking, it will carry out the mistake faithfully. Read what it hands you before you say yes, the way you’d check a draft before signing it.

Two things it still cannot do on its own: it cannot spend money or buy anything (there is no purchase feature, payment fields are refused in code, and anything shaped like paying on a website is stopped and routed to you first) and unprompted it can only ever message you, never your team’s channels. The one way words it wrote reach anyone else is a reply, to an email or a text, that you read and press Send on, which then goes out from your own account as you.

Untrusted text can reach your agent, and the gate won’t fully fix it.

If your agent reads a Slack attachment, a meeting transcript, or a web page, that text lands in front of it, and a hostile message could try to talk your agent into something you never asked for. This is a real class of attack against every AI agent, ours included, and we’re not going to pretend we’re exempt.

The approval gate stops such an attack from changing anything in your connected accounts that is not easily reversible. It does not stop everything: an injected instruction can still add items, write a note into your agent’s memory (where it would persist), and, worst of all, leak something, by having your agent fetch a web address or run a search whose text carries information from your conversation. We don’t have a complete answer to that yet. Nobody in this industry does. We’d rather write that sentence than let you assume we’d solved it.

Archie checks your plan, and it tells you exactly what that check sees.

Archie is a plan: $30 a month, or $299 a year. The app checks that plan when you sign in, so it isn’t a fully offline product, and we’re not going to dress that up: our servers see that your account has a current plan, and nothing more.

That means the honest answer to “what if I stop paying?” is that Archie stops letting you in, at the end of the period you have already paid for. Nothing on your computer is deleted, and starting a plan again puts you back where you were; if the payment system books your return under a fresh customer record, the restore can take an email to us before the plan is recognized, so write if anything looks stuck. We used to sell this outright and say so here; we changed it, and this paragraph changed with it rather than being left to age quietly.

There is a limit on how long Archie will run without hearing from us, and we would rather tell you the number than let you find it. When you sign in, our server hands the app a signed note saying what your account can open, and that note is good for 60 days. Every launch that can reach us replaces it, so in ordinary use it never runs down and you will never see this. But an Archie kept offline for two months will ask you to sign in again before it carries on. The note is signed because the alternative was a plain switch inside the app, which anyone could flip; making it unforgeable is what gives it an expiry date at all.

The other scenario is the one we have committed to in writing. If we disappear, Archie keeps working. Our Terms require that if Otian ever ceases operations, we publish a final version that requires no license check, within 30 days. It’s a term of the agreement, not a promise on a blog, so you don’t have to trust us for it. The two numbers are deliberate: the note lasts twice as long as the deadline for that final build, so the promise has a month of room in it rather than landing exactly as your copy stops.

What you’d lose if we vanished is updates, the marketplace, and support: the things a living company provides. You would not lose the agent you built. It’s on your disk, and it was never ours; your copy runs up to 60 days on its last license note, and the final build the Terms oblige us to publish is what keeps it running past that.

That matters more than it sounds. Personal-AI apps get acquired, pivoted, and switched off all the time, and when they go, their users’ data tends to leave with them. Yours can’t: there was never a copy on our side to take, sell, or shut off.

We keep a receipt for every paid add-on.

Buy a paid add-on and we store a permanent record: which one, how much, and when. It’s how we know to let you re-install it on a new computer. But it does mean we know which paid add-ons you own.

A free add-on leaves no receipt. Adding one bumps its public install count, signed in as you so the tally can’t be gamed, but we keep no record of which free add-ons are yours.

Nobody has audited us but us.

We have no third-party penetration test and no SOC 2 report. We’re a two-person team, and we’re saying so up front: you deserve to know exactly where we stand before you trust us with anything.

What we can offer instead is below: don’t trust us. Check.

Don’t Trust Us

Check for yourself. It takes 10 minutes.

Everything on the Trust page is a claim, and claims are cheap. Here is how to prove or disprove ours without taking our word for a single thing.

1

Install a network monitor.

LuLu is free and open-source. Little Snitch is paid and friendlier. Either one shows you every connection an app on your Mac tries to make, and lets you block them.

2

Open Archie and use it properly.

Sign in. Install an add-on. Give your agent a real task: something with a file, or your calendar. Let it run. Then read the list of connections it made.

3

Here is exactly what you should see.

If you see anything else carrying your content, we have either lied to you or made a serious mistake, and we want to hear about it either way.

  • api.anthropic.com, api.openai.com, api.groq.com,
    api.x.ai, generativelanguage.googleapis.com,
    api.deepseek.com, api.mistral.ai, or the address you typed for another provider: your agent thinking, on your key. Whichever one you connected, and only that one.
  • archie-4f35.onrender.com: our billing service, and the proxy for the free credits you start with. Once your own key is in, your agent stops going near it.
  • firestore.googleapis.com
    securetoken.googleapis.com: our sign-in and plan check, the version ping and crash reports until you turn those off, the add-on catalog, and the phone mailbox if you enabled it. Carries your account ID and those records, never your content.
  • otianai.com: checking for an update, on launch, hourly, and when you come back to the window. Carries nothing about you.
  • assets.otianai.com: only when an add-on you install needs a tool downloaded, like a voice.
  • github.com: only if an update is downloading.
  • Plus whichever accounts you connected: Google, Slack, Telegram, Discord, Fireflies. Directly, on your tokens.
4

Now block us, and watch nothing happen.

Add otianai.com and archie-4f35.onrender.com to your firewall’s block list and your agent’s thinking carries on exactly as before. That is the entire argument, reduced to something you can test in thirty seconds: on your own key, nothing of ours is in that path, so cutting us out of it changes nothing about it. What stops is what those hosts honestly are: updates, new tool downloads, and the periodic license renewal, so after about two months of blocking us Archie will refuse to start agents until it can check in once. Try the test before you connect a key and the free credits stop instead, because that one path really does run through us, exactly as the second line of the list above says.

Where we think this ends up. The real answer to “why should I believe you” is an open-source client, so that none of this rests on our word. We’re not there yet, and we’re not going to describe a plan as though it were a fact. For now: the monitor, the block list, and a company that would rather be corrected than trusted by default.

The Marketplace

Why an add-on can’t reach your files.

The frightening version of a marketplace is: you install a stranger’s plugin, and it runs code on your computer, next to your email. That is not what this is, and the reason is structural, not a promise.

Archie has nowhere to run code. A Skill is a text file plus some settings. A Personality is a set of written instructions. A Routine is a schedule. Nothing in an add-on can run as a program, so an add-on cannot itself read your disk or open a network connection. Not because we’d catch it; because there is no mechanism for it to use. What it can do is instruct your agent, which reads only what you have granted it and can fetch public web pages, so a malicious add-on has the same leak channel as any hostile text your agent reads. Treat installed instructions with the same care as anything else you let your agent read; the prompt-injection admission above is about add-ons too.

What an add-on can do is tell your agent how to behave, and declare which of your connected accounts it needs. A calendar Skill gets calendar tools. Two honest edges to that. Declaring is what narrows: an add-on that declares nothing, like plain chat, can reach every service you have connected. And the grant is blunter than we want: declaring “calendar” grants reading, creating, and deleting together, rather than asking you about each, capped only by the account itself, because a calendar connected with reading alone never yields the create or delete tools to anything. Splitting the grant apart, and showing you in plain English what an add-on is asking for before you install it, is part of the same work as the approval gate above.

Every add-on is read by a human before it is listed. Right now that human is one of the two of us, and we read every line of every submission. That will not scale forever. When it stops being true, this paragraph will change; we won’t quietly leave it here.
